clue.text: Only one Labour leader for us — Mr Miliband's ditched

indicators.note: one thing standing for another means it takes the other's place in the word

parts.note: only, as in 'only just', means barely: just
the letters of the word us are the ones swapped out
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: Ed Miliband led the Labour Party from 2010 to 2015

explanation.surface: A Labour supporter laments that only one Miliband brother could lead, so the other was dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' means one thing replaces another inside the 'only' word. The surface recalls the 2010 leadership contest in which Ed Miliband beat his brother David.
explanation.definitionFit: To be jilted is to be abruptly abandoned by a lover, which is being ditched.

clue.text: Sister and boyfriend trapped in island swamps

indicators.note: one thing trapped in another sits inside it, so the island's letters go round the rest

parts.note: a sister in a convent is a nun
a date is the person you are going out with

explanation.surface: A nun and her boyfriend stranded on an island, something of a scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: To inundate is to flood, and swamps used as a verb also means floods or overwhelms.

clue.text: Sleeveless jacket and dull 'eadgear used up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the letters are read bottom to top, i.e. backwards

parts.note: drab means dull or colourless
headgear with its H dropped, Cockney style, is a hat without the H

explanation.surface: Someone's shabby outfit: a sleeveless jacket and a dull, worn-out hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ''eadgear' tells you to drop the H from HAT, leaving AT. DRAB plus AT, reversed by 'used up', gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabard is a sleeveless tunic, worn historically by heralds and knights over armour.

clue.text: Possibly winning outsider ineligible for the Scots Greys?

definitions.meaning: a little-known contender who may yet unexpectedly win
the Scots Greys were a cavalry regiment mounted only on grey horses, so a black or brown mount would not qualify

explanation.surface: A racing tip about an unfancied runner, with an aside about cavalry.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Scots Greys, a British cavalry regiment, took their name from their grey horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark horse is an unexpected contender with hidden ability, and literally a horse not grey.

clue.text: Cast from violent western short of energy

indicators.note: violent suggests a wild disturbance, so the remaining letters are thrown into a new order
short of means lacking, so the letter is removed

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A cast taken from a violent western film, but one lacking energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove an E from WESTERN to leave WSTERN, then 'violent' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Strewn and cast are both past participles meaning scattered or thrown about.

clue.text: Boy in charge of sound …

parts.note: a boy is a son

explanation.surface: A boy put in charge of the sound, at a gig perhaps, with the ellipsis linking to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonic is an adjective meaning relating to sound waves or audible noise.

clue.text: … rings those limiting EastEnders in series

indicators.note: the limiting letters go in the series word

parts.note: rounds are a series, as of drinks or a competition

indicators.note: the letters limiting a word are its outermost two, at either end

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue: a sound person rings round the EastEnders cast for a series.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a long-running BBC soap opera set in east London; 'rings' looks like a phone call but is the verb for echoing.
explanation.definitionFit: Resounds means echoes or rings out loudly, as a bell or a hall does.

clue.text: Least good material editor's disposed of

indicators.note: something disposed of is got rid of, so it comes out of the word

parts.note: worsted is a woollen fabric
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: An editor has thrown out the worst cloth from a stock of material.
explanation.definitionFit: Worst is the superlative of bad, the opposite end from best, hence least good.

clue.text: Drop off small logs

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
lumber is timber cut into logs or planks

explanation.surface: An instruction to deliver some small logs.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop off is to fall asleep, and to slumber is to sleep.

clue.text: A new church first raised in power in formal measure

indicators.note: first places the raised-in-power word at the front, ahead of the other pieces

parts.note: a number raised to the power of two is squared
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A newly built church is raised up in power, in a formal ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' is an old word for a dance; the square dance is formal in its set figures.
explanation.definitionFit: A measure is an old term for a stately dance, and this one is formally patterned in sets of four couples.

clue.text: Anticipating endless warbling, son retires for a breather

indicators.note: anticipating means coming before, so the son piece goes first
retiring means going back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: the word son taken as written

indicators.note: endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: a trill is a warbled, quavering run of notes in birdsong

explanation.surface: A son steps out for a breather before the endless warbling starts.
explanation.walkthrough: A trill is a warble in birdsong or singing; cutting its last L leaves TRIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostril is literally an organ one breathes through, a playful sense of breather.

clue.text: Biblical petition (Parry's older translation)

indicators.note: a translation turns words into another form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the S of the possessive is kept as a letter here

explanation.surface: Hubert Parry's setting of an older translation of a biblical prayer, an apt choral picture.
explanation.walkthrough: Hubert Parry was an English composer of church music, best known for 'Jerusalem'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord's Prayer, taught by Jesus in the Gospels, is a petition addressed to God.

clue.text: Clandestine subject to Basie about backing

parts.note: under means subject to, as in under orders
the jazz bandleader Count Basie was known as the Count

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A secret jazz matter: someone under Count Basie's orders, backing his band.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods sold beneath the shop counter are sold secretly or illicitly, so the idiom means clandestine.

clue.text: Posh hotel in eastern half of French resort

indicators.note: on a map the eastern half is the right-hand half, so the western letters are dropped

parts.note: Biarritz is a seaside resort in south-west France

explanation.surface: A smart hotel located in the eastern part of a French seaside town.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ritz in London and Paris is a byword for luxury, so it is the archetypal posh hotel.

clue.text: Coarse flour is presumably not called for

definitions.meaning: flour that is coarse has been milled less finely, read whimsically as a two-word phrase

explanation.surface: A baker's observation that coarse flour is not needed in a recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: coarse flour is 'ground less', split into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something groundless has no basis or justification, so it is uncalled for.

clue.text: Catholic film studios

definitions.meaning: with a capital disguising it, catholic means all-embracing or worldwide

explanation.surface: A Catholic film studio, perhaps making religious epics.
explanation.definitionFit: Catholic in its lower-case sense means wide-ranging and all-inclusive, the same as worldwide.

clue.text: Found limited joy in running heats

indicators.note: the joy piece goes in the middle of the rearranged letters
running suggests things being in motion and mixed up, so the letters are rearranged
limited means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: bliss is great joy

explanation.surface: An athlete found only limited joy in running the heats.
explanation.walkthrough: HEATS rearranged gives ESTAH; BLIS, joy cut short by 'limited', is inserted to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To found a company is to set it up, which is to establish it.

clue.text: Job that's boring, boring and fixed at sea

indicators.note: boring as in drilling into, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the word and taken as written
a chore is a tedious task

explanation.surface: A sailor's complaint about a dull job, endlessly tedious, while moored at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' appears twice: first describing the tedious job, then meaning drilling into AND.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship anchored is held fast in position at sea by its anchor.

clue.text: Island is in her itinerary, not entirely cut off

indicators.note: the answer is drawn from the words but uses only part of them, not all

explanation.surface: A travel note: an island is on her itinerary, though not all of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer starts at the last letter of 'Island' and runs into 'itinerary'.
explanation.definitionFit: To disinherit someone is to cut them off from an inheritance.

clue.text: Step up or down without a movement

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letter is taken out

parts.note: a stair is a step one goes up or down

explanation.surface: A dance instruction: step up or down, but do not move.
explanation.definitionFit: A stir is a slight movement, as in 'not a stir in the house'.

clue.text: Eg the Guardian reported a bloomer

indicators.note: reported means heard said, so the answer sounds like this word

parts.note: the Guardian is an example of a daily newspaper

explanation.surface: The Guardian has reported a blunder, a bloomer being a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a blunder, a word the Guardian's misprints made famous, but here it is a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A dahlia is a garden plant grown for its showy flowers, so playfully something that blooms.

clue.text: Austen's ultimate representation of rare bygone Bath?

definitions.text: Austen's ultimate representation of rare bygone Bath?

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so only the final letter of the name is used
a representation renders something in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Austen's final novel depicts old Bath, rare and bygone.
explanation.walkthrough: The final N of Austen precedes an anagram of RAREBYGONEBATH. The novel, published after Austen's death, is largely set in Georgian Bath, a spa city in Somerset.
explanation.definitionFit: This Gothic parody by Jane Austen, published posthumously, has much of its action in Bath.

clue.text: Runner's livelier without one

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letter comes out

parts.note: racier means livelier or more spirited
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A runner is livelier without carrying anything extra.
explanation.definitionFit: A racer is a competitor in a race, someone or something that runs.

clue.text: Mad mongrel decapitated in New York

indicators.note: the shortened dog goes in the middle of the abbreviation
decapitated means the head, the first letter, is cut off

parts.note: a mutt is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A crazed stray dog gets its head cut off in New York, a lurid tabloid story.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutty is informal for crazy or eccentric, so it means mad.

clue.text: Sample last of lager in bar

indicators.note: the single letter goes inside the word for bar

parts.note: bar as a preposition means except, as in 'all bar one'

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A drinker offered a taste of the lager in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, but here means except.
explanation.definitionFit: An excerpt is an extract, a sample taken from a longer piece.

clue.text: OAP guarded by senior army man

indicators.note: something guarded by another is surrounded by it

parts.note: an OAP, old-age pensioner, is an oldie

explanation.surface: A pensioner is protected by a senior army officer.
explanation.walkthrough: OAP is a British abbreviation for old-age pensioner.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier is a man or woman serving in an army.

clue.text: Skirmish grips papers for 24 hours

indicators.note: the outer word grips, holding the other inside it

parts.note: a fray is a fight or skirmish
ID, identity papers

explanation.surface: A skirmish grabs the newspapers' attention for a full day.
explanation.definitionFit: Friday is a day of the week, and each day spans twenty-four hours.

clue.text: See "hate" in another form

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see

indicators.note: putting the word into another form means its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to look up hate as a different word, like a dictionary cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: loathing is hate in another, stronger form.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe is to detest intensely, which is a more intense way of saying detest.
